title: The proofs behind the pictures
learning_goal: State Propositions 1-5 with their exact scope, as the specialists will want them, and see which picture of ch07-ch08 each one backs.
takeaway: Each picture of ch07-ch08 is backed by an elementary statement with a precise scope, often known in other forms.
notes: Extension module, extended cut only, inserted after 08.7 (before X3a and before the chapter's card ch08.Q, CONTRACT P1). All six scenes are ready (D4): no simulation, training or benchmark, no new data file. Data read from existing files only: data/e2_eval.json (X2.2: the plain generator's 0.408 and the three gauges 5.05e-17, 1.78e-17, 2.03e-8 at the test values of eta), data/e1_samples_0.85.json (X2.4: model C endpoints at Γ = 0.85), data/e1_samples_0.9.json and data/e1_finegrid.json (X2.5: the 8,000 reference snapshots, their dE/dt, and mu, nu). Register PAPER throughout: X2.1 carries the T3 ink change NIGHT -> PAPER in its 2.2-s lead-in (08.7 is NIGHT); X3.0 opens X3a on PAPER, so there is no change back; X2.Q stays on PAPER. Modules are asides: no chapter card; X2.1 shows the rail at L4 with no climb and a lower-third chapter tag 'EXTENSION X2 · LEVEL 4 · AN ASIDE'. A shared 'X2 strip' (scenes/X2/x2_strip.js) of five small cards tracks the five propositions across the module. Badges: PROVED on the five proposition scenes (notes: Prop. 1 trivial by design; Prop. 2 + Remark 3.6 with E2 gauges measured; Prop. 3 with the gap credited to Bastek et al. 2025; Prop. 4 classical, Köhler et al. 2020, consistent with E1; Prop. 5 + Remark 3.11, necessity classical, Echeverría 1982); none on the question card. P22 respected: the module opens on 'each is elementary; what matters is its exact scope', and the chips credit what is classical or known. CHANGES AGAINST THE OUTLINE, to review: (1) X2.2 50 -> 55 s: it gains the predict beat of Remark 3.6 ('exact pull plus a bounded error: does a stray part survive?', hold 2.5 s, PREDICT on screen), the most counterintuitive point of the module, and closes the loop with 08.2 ('the plain generator's zero point four one reads as a missing pull', hedged as the report's interpretation, R:1023); point (d) (stiffness, fixed steps) is on the formula layer only. (2) X2.3 uses the report's own counterexample (data at -1 and +1, the law x^2 = 1) in the strings picture, then generalises to the circle; it states that the flat sheet's penalty was linear, hence unbiased at the optimum but only approximate in practice (08.2, 08.6), and credits the gap on a chip. (3) X2.4 45 -> 50 s: adds the condition 'if each true crowd is symmetric' (critique C10), the cost (two passes; 0.5 vs 0.25 s per 1,000 samples on a chip) and the joint impeller-swap symmetry R_π of VKS (same proof, untested, R:1187), which sets up the card. (4) NEW question card X2.Q (category runs, ask C. Nore / Y. Ponty): can the asymmetry sweep be simulated at one sign only, the other being supplied by the built-in half-turn? It is distinct from ch07.Q (budgets) and ch08.Q (discrete operator); X4.5 and X6.4 show R_π as a criterion only. Its number n is left null: in the extended cut it falls between ch07.Q (Q8) and ch08.Q (Q9), so the question register (script/_shared) must renumber or use a module label. (5) X2.5 introduces the generator L and the degrees on screen only (critique B4; the narration says 'the equations give its rate of change'), uses the real Gissinger fixed point N+ (closed formula, P4:389; unstable saddle-focus, P4:1532) and draws the unstable loop as SCHEMATIC. Module duration: outline 3:30; targets now 3:56 with the card after the adversarial review (X2.2 57 s, X2.3 42 s, X2.4 53 s; see script/_review/X2.md). SYMBOL SHEET: Π for the orthogonal projector (the report's P would clash with the injection rate P of 08.5); 'Dec' for the decoder (the report's calligraphic C would clash with model C and the classes C1-C4, which stay in 08.6); ker A instead of S for the subspace (S is the dials' mirror of ch07); no R^D (D is the dipole); mu, mu_λ allowed here (symbol sheet: X2 and X4); q violet, t transport time, v violet, λ and Γ green, crowd laws amber; Lip not used. LEXICON: no new word ('Jensen', 'equivariant', 'impellers' are plain English; no Greek letter is spoken). Words budgeted with the assembler formula (146 raw words per minute, 0.9 s per paragraph break, holds, lead-in and tail). sentences.text: An aside: the five statements behind the pictures.
Each is elementary; what matters is its exact scope.
The first is almost too simple.
Suppose every field a {model}decoder{/} can draw obeys a linear law, like zero divergence.
Then every sample obeys it, whatever the {model}crowd of codes{/}, however badly trained.
The proof is one line.
The work is in the decoder: hill maps in two dimensions, a vector potential in three, with its gauge fixed.

sentences.text: Second: the spring, in full.
If the data lie in a flat subspace, the ideal {model}wind{/} splits in two.
Along it, a part a network can learn.
Across it, a pull back: the stray part, divided by the time left on the clock.
Followed exactly, that pull lands every sample in the subspace.
Trained perfectly, the plain generator, both projections and hill maps give the same crowd.
Cap the pull, and an order-one stray part survives.
Now add a small, bounded error to the exact pull. Does a stray part survive?
No. The pull erases it.
So the plain generator's zero point four one reads as a missing pull, not a small error.
And the projected flow's tiny residue? Single precision.

sources: en/rapport/index.qmd:342 (Proposition 2 explains why several different mechanisms aim at the same target, and where the residual divergence of a model that enforces nothing comes from; elementary, probably known in other forms)

en/rapport/index.qmd:345-360 (Proposition 2: S a subspace, P the orthogonal projector, mu(S) = 1, x0 ~ N(0, I) independent of x1 ~ mu; v* = m(Px, t) − (I − P)x/(1 − t), m in S; (a) (I − P)x(t) = (1 − t)(I − P)x(0), the final sample is exactly in S; (b) with perfect training, free generation, final projection, projected flow and potentials give the same distribution, the observed differences come from approximation error and inductive bias, not from the target; (c) a contraction rate bounded by K and a residual bounded by rho leave ||(I − P)x(1)|| ≥ e^-K ||(I − P)x(0)|| − rho, a residual divergence of order one; (d) the term is stiff near t = 1, an explicit fixed-step scheme resolves it poorly over the last steps)
en/rapport/index.qmd:362-371 (proof of Proposition 2)

en/rapport/index.qmd:376-377 (Remark 3.6: an error added to the exact field, ||r|| ≤ rho, gives y(t) = (1 − t)[y(0) + ∫ r/(1 − s)], second term bounded by rho (1 − t) ln(1/(1 − t)) → 0, the contraction erases the error; a finite divergence comes from the missing rate 1/(1 − t) plus the finite step; the E2 free-generation divergence should be read as a failure to represent the stiff term, not as a small uniform error)
en/rapport/index.qmd:380-386 (explicit example: a bounded term along S, a term −y2/(1 − t) across it that diverges as t → 1)

en/rapport/index.qmd:645 (V3: the noise x0 is projected during training as well, so the network only learns the field m of Proposition 2; V3 works in single precision, which sets its residual divergence at the rounding level)

left.path_note: the ideal path through x_t = 0 is flat from the noise point x = 0: by symmetry the ideal wind E[x1 - x0 | x_t = 0] is zero on that line for every t < 1, so its guess is 0

moved_path.note: ideal guess E[x1 | x_t] = tanh(t x_t / (1 - t)^2) = tanh(0.6), about 0.54, strictly between 0 and +1; the penalty (x^2 - 1)^2 on the guess pushes it outward toward +1 (R:394: the derivative is non-zero where 0 < guess < 1); drawn SCHEMATIC, ghost = ideal path at 25 %

sentences.text: Third: penalties. A common one tests the {model}model's guess{/} of where its path will end.
With the ideal wind, that guess averages the data that could lie ahead.
For a linear law, an average of lawful fields is lawful: the penalty vanishes at the optimum, and moves nothing.
Off the optimum, in a real network, it holds the law only roughly.
For a curved law, that fails: two points on a circle average to a point inside.
This is the Jensen gap: now the penalty biases the optimum itself.

sentences.text: Fourth: the mirror, as a theorem.
Make the {model}wind{/} equivariant: mirror a point, and its arrow mirrors too.
Start from noise that looks the same in the mirror.
Then every path has a mirror twin.
So the generated crowd is exactly symmetric at every {param}knob setting{/}, even with lopsided or missing data.
If every true crowd is symmetric, averaging a wind with its mirror never raises the expected loss.
The cost: two network passes instead of one.
In the VKS cylinder, a half-turn swapping the two impellers is a second symmetry.
If their speeds differ, it also flips the sign of that difference, the {param}forcing asymmetry{/}.
The same proof covers it, untested so far.

sentences.text: Last, crowd laws. The equations give any quantity a rate of change at each snapshot.
If the crowd is stationary, that rate {metric}averages to zero{/}, for every quantity; the energy budget is one case.
The proof: let every snapshot run for a moment.
The crowd looks the same, so no average moves: the mean rate is zero.
Necessary, not sufficient: a crowd parked on an unstable fixed point passes every such test.
So does an unstable loop.
The fit to data must therefore stay in the loss.

question.say: Can we simulate only one sign of forcing asymmetry, and let the impeller swap supply the other?
question.fr: Peut-on ne simuler qu'un seul signe de l'asymétrie de forçage, et laisser l'échange des turbines fournir l'autre ?
question.why: Built into the network, the half-turn makes the crowd at negative asymmetry the exact image of the crowd at positive asymmetry: that could halve the asymmetry runs, if impellers, materials and mesh are truly swap-symmetric.
question.unblocks: Runs: one sign or both in the asymmetry sweep. Framing: which symmetries the generator builds in (two or four network passes), and whether the meridian mesh must be symmetric.
question.why_fr: Intégré au réseau, le demi-tour rend la foule à asymétrie négative image exacte de la foule à asymétrie positive : de quoi diviser par deux les runs d'asymétrie, si turbines, matériaux et maillage sont vraiment symétriques par échange.
question.unblocks_fr: Runs : un seul signe ou les deux dans le balayage d'asymétrie. Cadrage : quelles symétries le générateur intègre (deux ou quatre passes du réseau), et si le maillage méridien doit être symétrique.
